title: Ezekiel 1 — The throne-vision by the Kebar canal

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֣י ׀ בִּשְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים שָׁנָ֗ה בָּֽרְבִיעִי֙ בַּחֲמִשָּׁ֣ה לַחֹ֔דֶשׁ וַאֲנִ֥י בְתֽוֹךְ־הַגּוֹלָ֖ה עַל־נְהַר־כְּבָ֑ר נִפְתְּחוּ֙ הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וָאֶרְאֶ֖ה מַרְא֥וֹת אֱלֹהִֽים׃

i18n.en: In the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth of the month, while I was among the exiles by the river Kebar, the skies were opened, and I saw visions of Elohim.

paragraphs.commentary: **The book opens on a date that is not exactly dated.** *Bishloshim shanah* — *in the thirtieth year*. The Hebrew gives no anchor for what the thirty years count *from*. Three readings circulate: (1) Ezekiel's age, as Levitical priests entered service at thirty (Num 4:3); the prophet-priest, displaced from Jerusalem and the Temple, is at the canonical age for cultic ministry — but in the wrong place. (2) The thirtieth year from Josiah's reform (which would place the vision in 593 BCE, matching v2's fifth year of Yoyakhin's exile). (3) The thirtieth year of a regnal cycle. The chapter does not specify; the unanchored date is itself a textual feature. // *Niftechu ha-shamayim* — *the skies were opened*. The verb is niphal (passive) — *something opens* the skies, agency unstated. The phrase recurs in Hebrew Bible vision-reports (cf. Acts 7:56 in the NT — Stephen sees the *opened* skies). The opening is a one-time event, not an ongoing state. // *Mar'ot Elohim* — *visions of Elohim*. The noun *mar'ah* (vision) is plural here — multiple visions, not a single image. The genitive *Elohim* is grammatically plural and is read in the WoH translation as the same plural class-noun as throughout the Hebrew Bible (see [`elohim-as-translation`](/wiki/elohim/)). 'Visions of Elohim' preserves both ambiguities — the multiplicity of the visions and the plural form of the divine class-noun. // *Tokh ha-gola* — *among the exiles*. Ezekiel is writing from inside the Babylonian deportation community. The vision happens in *Babylonia*, not Jerusalem — a structural detail the chapter emphasizes through repetition (v1 *al-nehar Kevar*, v3 *b'eretz Kasdim al-nehar Kevar*).

paragraphs.text: בַּחֲמִשָּׁ֖ה לַחֹ֑דֶשׁ הִ֚יא הַשָּׁנָ֣ה הַחֲמִישִׁ֔ית לְגָל֖וּת הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ יוֹיָכִֽין׃

i18n.en: On the fifth of the month — this was the fifth year of the exile of King Yoyakhin —

paragraphs.commentary: **A second dating, in a different voice.** Where v1 was first-person (*va'ani b'tokh ha-gola* — *I was among the exiles*), v2-3 are third-person — an editorial gloss inserted into the prophet's own opening. The two dating systems coexist: the unanchored 'thirtieth year' of v1 and the precise 'fifth year of Yoyakhin's exile' of v2. The latter dates the vision to **593 BCE** by modern reconstructions of the Babylonian chronology. // *Yoyakhin* (יוֹיָכִין) was the penultimate king of Judah, deported to Babylon in 597 BCE in the first Babylonian deportation; the chapter is locating the vision in the early years of the Babylonian Exile, ~6 years before the destruction of the Temple in 587/586 BCE. Modern English Bibles often render the name as *Jehoiachin*; the WoH translation preserves *Yoyakhin* as closer to the Hebrew.

paragraphs.text: הָיֹ֣ה הָיָ֣ה דְבַר־יְ֠הוָה אֶל־יְחֶזְקֵ֨אל בֶּן־בּוּזִ֧י הַכֹּהֵ֛ן בְּאֶ֥רֶץ כַּשְׂדִּ֖ים עַל־נְהַר־כְּבָ֑ר וַתְּהִ֥י עָלָ֛יו שָׁ֖ם יַד־יְהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: the word of YHWH came indeed to Ezekiel son of Buzi the priest, in the land of the Kasdim, by the river Kebar; and there the hand of YHWH was upon him.

paragraphs.commentary: **The prophet's full identification.** Three pieces of information are loaded into one verse. // *Yehezkel ben Buzi ha-kohen* — *Ezekiel son of Buzi the priest*. Ezekiel is a priestly-lineage figure (a *kohen*, descendant of Aaron), exiled from the Temple in Jerusalem to Babylonia. The priestly identity is structurally important: Ezekiel's prophetic-vision register is also *priestly* in a way that contrasts with the prophetic-rhetorical register of Jeremiah (his contemporary, in Jerusalem). The chapter is being recorded by someone whose first language is Temple-cultic-spatial. // *B'eretz Kasdim* — *in the land of the Kasdim* (the Chaldeans). Same chronologically-mixed term as Gen 11:28, 31 ('Ur of the Kasdim' — see glossary entry `ur-kasdim`): *Kasdim* is the first-millennium-BCE Aramean people who came to dominate Babylonia in the Neo-Babylonian period. // *Yad-YHWH alav* — *the hand of YHWH was upon him*. The phrase is a technical Ezekiel-formula for the onset of prophetic experience (recurs at 3:14, 3:22, 8:1, 33:22, 37:1, 40:1). *Yad* (hand) is anthropomorphic but also covers the broader sense of *power, agency, custody* — the prophet is taken-hold-of.

paragraphs.text: וָאֵ֡רֶא וְהִנֵּה֩ ר֨וּחַ סְעָרָ֜ה בָּאָ֣ה מִן־הַצָּפ֗וֹן עָנָ֤ן גָּדוֹל֙ וְאֵ֣שׁ מִתְלַקַּ֔חַת וְנֹ֥גַֽהּ ל֖וֹ סָבִ֑יב וּמִ֨תּוֹכָ֔הּ כְּעֵ֥ין הַחַשְׁמַ֖ל מִתּ֥וֹךְ הָאֵֽשׁ׃

i18n.en: I looked, and behold — a stormy wind was coming from the north, a great cloud with flashing fire, and brightness around it; and from the middle of it — like the look of *chashmal*, from the middle of the fire.

paragraphs.commentary: **The opening apparition.** The verse stacks five descriptors of a single phenomenon approaching from the north: (1) a *stormy wind* (*ruach se'arah*); (2) a *great cloud* (*anan gadol*); (3) *flashing fire* (*esh mitlaqachat*); (4) *brightness* (*nogah*) around it; (5) at its center, the appearance of ***chashmal*** from the middle of the fire. // The phenomenon is **coming from the north**. The Hebrew Bible's geographic-mythic north (*tzafon*) is the direction of the divine mountain in Canaanite tradition (Mount Zaphon / Jebel al-Aqra in Syria, the seat of Baal); it is also the direction from which the great Mesopotamian empires (Assyria, Babylon) historically invaded the Levant. Ezekiel is writing from Babylonia, and the vision approaches from a yet-more-northerly direction — beyond Babylon, in the cosmic-north register. // ***Chashmal*** (חַשְׁמַל) — the chapter's most contested term. The word appears in the Hebrew Bible only here (Ezek 1:4, 1:27) and in Ezek 8:2; it has no clear Hebrew etymology. The LXX renders ἤλεκτρον (*elektron* — electrum, the gold-silver alloy used for cultic vessels and royal regalia in ANE contexts; Akkadian *elmešu* may be cognate). Modern English splits: KJV/ASV 'amber'; NJPS 'electrum'; NRSV 'gleaming amber'; ESV 'gleaming metal'. The Vulgate uses *electrum*. // The lexical core is something **metallic, gleaming, fire-bright** — the chapter uses the Hebrew expression *ke-ein* ('like the look of') to flag that even Ezekiel is describing by analogy: this is what it *looked like*. Modern Hebrew uses *chashmal* for *electricity*, a 19th-century reuse by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda — the biblical word was the natural Hebrew for a luminous-electrical phenomenon. The WoH translation preserves the Hebrew form (*chashmal*) untranslated, parallel to how *Elohim* is preserved. The reader meets the chapter's own technical vocabulary on the page. // The *ke-ein* hedging-formula recurs throughout the chapter — Ezekiel reports appearances and likenesses, not identifications. The discipline is a translator's gift: the chapter teaches the reader to read what is said, not what is meant.

paragraphs.text: וּמִ֨תּוֹכָ֔הּ דְּמ֖וּת אַרְבַּ֣ע חַיּ֑וֹת וְזֶה֙ מַרְאֵֽיהֶ֔ן דְּמ֥וּת אָדָ֖ם לָהֵֽנָּה׃

i18n.en: And from the middle of it — the likeness of four living creatures. And this was their appearance: they had the likeness of human.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chayyot emerge from the middle of the fire.** *Demut arba chayyot* — *the likeness of four living creatures*. The chapter uses *demut* (likeness) rather than direct identification — Ezekiel is describing what he sees by way of resemblance. // *Chayyot* (חַיּוֹת) is from the root *chai* — *alive, living*. The same root is *chayyah* (life, animal), *chayyim* (life-plural). The plural *chayyot* here names creatures-with-life: animate, but not necessarily *biological-animal* in the sense the rest of the Hebrew Bible uses *chayyah* for cattle and wild animals. The English convention 'living creatures' is acceptable; 'living beings' is also defensible. The chapter uses *chayyot* as a technical class-noun for the figures, not as the generic biological term. // *Demut adam lahennah* — *they had the likeness of human*. The four figures are *adam*-like in form. The chapter is staging the vision in the canonical Hebrew Bible vocabulary: *demut* and *tselem* (image) were established in Gen 1:26-27 as the relational-categorial vocabulary linking *adam* and *Elohim*. Ezekiel's chayyot are now described in the same *demut*-vocabulary. The relational geometry is being staged.

paragraphs.text: וְאַרְבָּעָ֥ה פָנִ֖ים לְאֶחָ֑ת וְאַרְבַּ֥ע כְּנָפַ֖יִם לְאַחַ֥ת לָהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: Each had four faces, and each had four wings.

paragraphs.commentary: **Four faces, four wings, per chayyah.** The numerology is precise: 4 × 4 + 4 × 4 — sixteen faces and sixteen wings across the four chayyot. The number *four* is the chapter's structural signature: four chayyot, four faces each, four wings each (in v6; reduced to two pairs in v11), four wheels (v15), four directions of motion (v9, v12, v17, v20). Four is the number of geographic directionality in Hebrew Bible cosmology (four winds, four corners of the earth, four rivers of Eden); the chayyot's design is calibrated to omnidirectional simultaneous-motion.

paragraphs.text: וְרַגְלֵיהֶ֖ם רֶ֣גֶל יְשָׁרָ֑ה וְכַ֣ף רַגְלֵיהֶ֗ם כְּכַף֙ רֶ֣גֶל עֵ֔גֶל וְנֹ֣צְצִ֔ים כְּעֵ֖ין נְחֹ֥שֶׁת קָלָֽל׃

i18n.en: Their legs were straight; the sole of their foot was like the sole of a calf's foot, and they gleamed like the look of burnished bronze.

paragraphs.commentary: **The legs, the feet, the burnished bronze.** *Regel yesharah* — *a straight leg* (not bent at a knee in human-anatomical fashion). *Kaf raglehem k'kaf regel egel* — *the sole of their foot like the sole of a calf's foot* (cleft-hoofed). The chayyot have the bipedal upright stance of human (*demut adam*, v5) but the lower-anatomy of cattle. // *Nochetzim ke-ein nechoshet qalal* — *gleaming like the look of burnished bronze*. *Qalal* (קָלָל) is a hapax adjective; the lexical sense is *polished, gleaming, smoothed*. The bronze register adds to v4's *chashmal* — this is metallic-gleaming-luminous throughout.

paragraphs.text: וידו [וִידֵ֣י] אָדָ֗ם מִתַּ֙חַת֙ כַּנְפֵיהֶ֔ם עַ֖ל אַרְבַּ֣עַת רִבְעֵיהֶ֑ם וּפְנֵיהֶ֥ם וְכַנְפֵיהֶ֖ם לְאַרְבַּעְתָּֽם׃

i18n.en: And the hands of human were under their wings on their four sides; and the faces and the wings of the four of them were thus:

paragraphs.commentary: **Ketiv/qere at the verse opening.** The consonantal text (ketiv) reads *vidav* (וִידוֹ — singular 'his hand'); the Masoretic vocalization (qere) reads *videi* (וִידֵי — plural 'hands of'). The chapter accepts the qere reading: *videi adam* — *hands of human*. // The figure now has: human-like form (v5), straight legs and calf's feet (v7), gleaming metallic surface (v7), human hands under the wings (v8). The body is composite — human in some parts, cattle-like in others, gleaming-metallic throughout. Ezekiel is describing what he sees by composite-likeness.

paragraphs.text: חֹֽבְרֹ֛ת אִשָּׁ֥ה אֶל־אֲחוֹתָ֖הּ כַּנְפֵיהֶ֑ם לֹא־יִסַּ֣בּוּ בְלֶכְתָּ֔ן אִ֛ישׁ אֶל־עֵ֥בֶר פָּנָ֖יו יֵלֵֽכוּ׃

i18n.en: Their wings were joined one to another; they would not turn as they went; each would go in the direction of its face.

paragraphs.commentary: **Wings joined, no-turning motion.** *Chovrot ishah el achotah* — literally *joined a woman to her sister*, the idiomatic Hebrew for *joined one to another* (the feminine grammatical agreement reflects that *knafayim* — wings — is feminine in Hebrew, not that the wings are female). The chayyot are linked into a single moving unit. // *Lo yissabu b'lekhtan* — *they would not turn as they went*. The chayyot move without rotation. *Ish el-ever panav yelekhu* — *each toward the side of its face would go*. Combined with the four-face design (v6, v10), the system has omnidirectional motion without ever rotating: the chayyot do not need to turn because they always have a face pointing in any direction they may need to go. This is a mechanical-design observation, not a metaphysical one.

paragraphs.text: וּדְמ֣וּת פְּנֵיהֶם֮ פְּנֵ֣י אָדָם֒ וּפְנֵ֨י אַרְיֵ֤ה אֶל־הַיָּמִין֙ לְאַרְבַּעְתָּ֔ם וּפְנֵי־שׁ֥וֹר מֵֽהַשְּׂמֹ֖אול לְאַרְבַּעְתָּ֑ן וּפְנֵי־נֶ֖שֶׁר לְאַרְבַּעְתָּֽן׃

i18n.en: The likeness of their faces: the face of human, and the face of a lion on the right side for the four of them, and the face of an ox on the left side for the four of them, and the face of an eagle for the four of them.

paragraphs.commentary: **The four faces named.** Each chayyah has four faces, each face oriented in a specific direction relative to the figure: human face (front, implied), lion-face right, ox-face left, eagle-face (rear, implied — though the chapter does not specify). The four faces are the four canonical 'rulers' of ANE biological hierarchy: human (king of intellect), lion (king of beasts), ox (king of domesticated/agricultural), eagle (king of birds). // The same four-face configuration recurs in Ezek 10:14 (with *cherub* replacing *human/ox* — a textual variation that has been read both as scribal corruption and as deliberate development across the book). The Christian tradition later read the four faces as symbolic of the four Gospels (the *tetramorph*); the four-face cherub motif goes back to Mesopotamian iconography (the *karibu* / *cherub* — winged composite guardian figures flanking thrones and temples). // The WoH translation preserves the literal animal-faces. The standard reading is that the four-face design is a representation of *totality* — the chayyot embody the comprehensive biological hierarchy of life, configured for omnidirectional motion.

paragraphs.text: וּפְנֵיהֶ֕ם וְכַנְפֵיהֶ֥ם פְּרֻד֖וֹת מִלְמָ֑עְלָה לְאִ֗ישׁ שְׁ֚תַּיִם חֹבְר֣וֹת אִ֔ישׁ וּשְׁתַּ֣יִם מְכַסּ֔וֹת אֵ֖ת גְּוִיֹתֵיהֶֽנָה׃

i18n.en: Their faces and their wings were separated from above; each had two wings joined to one another, and two covered their bodies.

paragraphs.commentary: **The wing configuration explained.** Of the four wings per chayyah (v6), two are joined to the neighboring chayyot's wings (linking the system into a single unit, per v9), and two cover the chayyah's own body. The two-up-two-down configuration is reminiscent of the seraphim of Isaiah 6:2 ('with two he covered his face, with two he covered his feet, with two he flew') — though Isaiah's seraphim have six wings to Ezekiel's four. The chapter is positioning the chayyot within the broader ANE throne-attendant iconography while maintaining their distinctive numeric signature.

paragraphs.text: וְאִ֛ישׁ אֶל־עֵ֥בֶר פָּנָ֖יו יֵלֵ֑כוּ אֶ֣ל אֲשֶׁר֩ יִֽהְיֶה־שָׁ֨מָּה הָר֤וּחַ לָלֶ֙כֶת֙ יֵלֵ֔כוּ לֹ֥א יִסַּ֖בּוּ בְּלֶכְתָּֽן׃

i18n.en: Each would go in the direction of its face. Wherever the ruach was about to go, they would go; they would not turn as they went.

paragraphs.commentary: ***Ha-ruach*** is the chapter's operating principle. The chayyot move *where the ruach is to go*. The Hebrew רוּחַ *ruach* has the same three-fold lexical field it had in Gen 1:2: *breath, wind, spirit*. In this chapter it functions as the *animating directive* of the chayyot-and-wheels system. // The chapter will return to this in v20-21: 'wherever the ruach was to go, they went; and the wheels were lifted up beside them, for the ruach of the chayyah was in the wheels'. The *ruach* is not external command but the very *animating force* embedded in the system itself. The chayyot do not have to be told where to go — the ruach in them directs the system as a unit. // The WoH lens reads this with attention: the chapter describes an integrated control-system, where the directive principle is internal to the apparatus. The translation preserves *ruach* as the technical noun rather than picking one of its three lexical fields prematurely; commentary surfaces the reading.

paragraphs.text: וּדְמ֨וּת הַחַיּ֜וֹת מַרְאֵיהֶ֣ם כְּגַחֲלֵי־אֵ֗שׁ בֹּֽעֲרוֹת֙ כְּמַרְאֵ֣ה הַלַּפִּדִ֔ים הִ֕יא מִתְהַלֶּ֖כֶת בֵּ֣ין הַחַיּ֑וֹת וְנֹ֣גַהּ לָאֵ֔שׁ וּמִן־הָאֵ֖שׁ יוֹצֵ֥א בָרָֽק׃

i18n.en: The likeness of the living creatures — their appearance was like burning coals of fire, like the appearance of torches; it was moving back and forth among the living creatures, and there was brightness to the fire, and from the fire lightning went forth.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chayyot as light-and-fire phenomenon.** *Gachalei esh bo'arot* — *burning coals of fire* — names the chayyot's surface appearance. The accompanying *lapidim* (*torches*) brings the imagery into the cultic register (torches are temple-ritual objects). *Boreq* (בָּרָק) — *lightning* — completes the discharge-description: there is brightness, and lightning issues from the fire. // The verse is the chapter's densest concentration of light-and-discharge vocabulary. Read with attention to the chapter's plainsense, the chayyot are luminous-fiery-bright objects emitting lightning. The Wheel of Heaven lens reads this with the technical reading available: *what kind of phenomenon emits brightness, contains fire, and discharges lightning?* The text preserves the description; commentary surfaces the questions.

paragraphs.text: וְהַחַיּ֖וֹת רָצ֣וֹא וָשׁ֑וֹב כְּמַרְאֵ֖ה הַבָּזָֽק׃

i18n.en: And the living creatures ran and returned, like the appearance of the flashing of lightning.

paragraphs.commentary: ***Ratso va-shov*** — *running and returning*. The verb-pair denotes rapid back-and-forth motion. The chayyot move *ke-mar'eh ha-bazaq* — *like the appearance of the flashing of lightning*. *Bazaq* (בָּזָק) is a hapax (occurring only here) but transparently related to *baraq* (בָּרָק, lightning, of v13). The figures move *as fast as lightning flashes*. The motion is staccato, not continuous flight.

paragraphs.text: וָאֵ֖רֶא הַחַיּ֑וֹת וְהִנֵּה֩ אוֹפַ֨ן אֶחָ֥ד בָּאָ֛רֶץ אֵ֥צֶל הַחַיּ֖וֹת לְאַרְבַּ֥עַת פָּנָֽיו׃

i18n.en: I looked at the living creatures, and behold — one wheel on the land beside the living creatures, for each of its four faces.

paragraphs.commentary: **The wheels enter the vision.** *Ofan* (אוֹפַן) is the standard Hebrew noun for *wheel* — the same word used for chariot-wheels, mill-wheels, and any rotating disc. The chapter pivots from the chayyot above to the wheels at ground level. // *Eretz* (אֶרֶץ) — *land* — anchors the wheels to the ground. The chayyot have appeared from above (v4 the storm-wind from the north, v5 from the middle of the cloud); the wheels are *al ha-aretz* (on the land). The system has both above-ground and ground-level components.

paragraphs.text: מַרְאֵ֨ה הָאוֹפַנִּ֤ים וּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם֙ כְּעֵ֣ין תַּרְשִׁ֔ישׁ וּדְמ֥וּת אֶחָ֖ד לְאַרְבַּעְתָּ֑ן וּמַרְאֵיהֶם֙ וּמַ֣עֲשֵׂיהֶ֔ם כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר יִהְיֶ֥ה הָאוֹפַ֖ן בְּת֥וֹךְ הָאוֹפָֽן׃

i18n.en: The appearance of the wheels and their workmanship was like the look of tarshish-stone, and the four of them had one likeness; and their appearance and their workmanship was as if a wheel were within a wheel.

paragraphs.commentary: **The wheel-within-wheel.** *Ka-asher yihyeh ha-ofan b'tokh ha-ofan* — *as if a wheel were within a wheel*. This is the chapter's most famous phrase outside of *chashmal*. The construction is one of Ezekiel's hedging-formulae (*ka-asher yihyeh* — 'as if it would be'); he is reporting what the wheels *looked like*, not asserting that wheels were literally inside wheels. // The standard scholarly reading is: two wheels intersecting at right angles, like the gimbal of a gyroscope or the orthogonal-axis wheels of a Ferris wheel — allowing the wheel-system to rotate in any direction without turning the chayyot above it. This matches the chapter's running concern with omnidirectional motion (v9, v12, v17). // *Ke-ein tarshish* — *like the look of tarshish-stone*. *Tarshish* (תַּרְשִׁישׁ) is a precious stone (Ex 28:20, Song 5:14, Dan 10:6) — variously identified with chrysolite, peridot, yellow jasper, or beryl. The classical-era association is golden-yellow / olive-gold. The chapter has now stacked three precious-substance descriptions on the apparatus: *chashmal* (electrum, v4 and v27), *nechoshet qalal* (burnished bronze, v7), and *tarshish* (here). The visual register is consistent: metallic-gleaming-luminous throughout.

paragraphs.text: עַל־אַרְבַּ֥עַת רִבְעֵיהֶ֖ן בְּלֶכְתָּ֣ם יֵלֵ֑כוּ לֹ֥א יִסַּ֖בּוּ בְּלֶכְתָּֽן׃

i18n.en: On their four sides they would go as they went; they would not turn as they went.

paragraphs.commentary: **The wheels share the chayyot's no-turning property.** The wheel-system and the chayyot-system move as a single unit: in any of four directions, without rotation. The mechanical observation is consistent across both sub-systems.

paragraphs.text: וְגַ֨בֵּיהֶ֔ן וְגֹ֥בַהּ לָהֶ֖ם וְיִרְאָ֣ה לָהֶ֑ם וְגַבֹּתָ֗ם מְלֵאֹ֥ת עֵינַ֛יִם סָבִ֖יב לְאַרְבַּעְתָּֽן׃

i18n.en: Their rims were high, and they were dreadful; and the rims of the four of them were full of eyes round about.

paragraphs.commentary: ***Gabbotam meleot einayim*** — *their rims were full of eyes*. *Gabbot* (גַּבּוֹת) is the plural of *gav* (back, rim) — the outer edge of the wheel. *Einayim* (eyes) names the multitude of sensors / aperture-like features distributed around the rim. // The phrase has been read at every level: literal eyes (the wheels as conscious-perceiving entities), gemstones glinting like eyes, sensors / detectors in the technical reading, or angelic-iconographic eye-motifs (the rims-full-of-eyes motif recurs in Christian art of the seraphim and in Revelation 4:6's four living creatures, who are themselves a re-reading of Ezekiel's chayyot). The chapter does not specify. The translation preserves the literal *einayim*; commentary surfaces the range. // *Gobah* (height) and *yir'ah* (dread, fear) compound: the rims are *tall* and *dreadful*. The word *yir'ah* is the Hebrew Bible's standard term for the appropriate human response to divine presence — the dread is here transferred to the wheels themselves, an extension of the sublime-as-machine-property.

paragraphs.text: וּבְלֶ֙כֶת֙ הַֽחַיּ֔וֹת יֵלְכ֥וּ הָאוֹפַנִּ֖ים אֶצְלָ֑ם וּבְהִנָּשֵׂ֤א הַֽחַיּוֹת֙ מֵעַ֣ל הָאָ֔רֶץ יִנָּשְׂא֖וּ הָאוֹפַנִּֽים׃

i18n.en: When the living creatures went, the wheels went beside them; and when the living creatures were lifted up from the land, the wheels were lifted up.

paragraphs.commentary: **The two sub-systems are mechanically coupled.** The wheels and the chayyot move together as a single unit, both in horizontal motion (*lekhet* — going) and vertical motion (*hinnase me'al ha-aretz* — being lifted up from the land). The chayyot can ascend (*hinnase*) off the ground, and the wheels rise with them. The verb *nasa* (lift, carry, raise) is the standard Hebrew term for *aerial elevation* — the chapter is describing the system's capacity for flight.

paragraphs.text: עַ֣ל אֲשֶׁר֩ יִֽהְיֶה־שָּׁ֨ם הָר֤וּחַ לָלֶ֙כֶת֙ יֵלֵ֔כוּ שָׁ֥מָּה הָר֖וּחַ לָלֶ֑כֶת וְהָאוֹפַנִּ֗ים יִנָּשְׂאוּ֙ לְעֻמָּתָ֔ם כִּ֛י ר֥וּחַ הַחַיָּ֖ה בָּאוֹפַנִּֽים׃

i18n.en: Wherever the ruach was about to go, they would go — there the ruach went to go; and the wheels were lifted up beside them, for the ruach of the living creature was in the wheels.

paragraphs.commentary: ***Ruach ha-chayyah ba-ofannim*** — *the ruach of the living-thing was in the wheels*. The chapter's most explicit statement of the integrated-control-system principle. The *ruach* that directs the chayyot's motion is *the same ruach* that operates the wheels — the two sub-systems share a single animating directive. The Hebrew preserves a precise distinction here: *chayyah* is singular (the living-thing), *ba-ofannim* (in the wheels) is plural. The system has *one* directive principle (singular ruach of chayyah) distributed across *multiple* parts (the four wheels). The chapter is describing a unified control architecture. // The verse is one of two (with v21) where the chapter most plainly states what the technical reading already suspects: this is an *integrated* apparatus, not a set of independent animate beings. The translation preserves the bare statement; commentary surfaces the architecture.

paragraphs.text: בְּלֶכְתָּ֣ם יֵלֵ֔כוּ וּבְעָמְדָ֖ם יַֽעֲמֹ֑דוּ וּֽבְהִנָּשְׂאָ֞ם מֵעַ֣ל הָאָ֗רֶץ יִנָּשְׂא֤וּ הָאֽוֹפַנִּים֙ לְעֻמָּתָ֔ם כִּ֛י ר֥וּחַ הַחַיָּ֖ה בָּאוֹפַנִּֽים׃

i18n.en: When they went, they went; when they stood, they stood; and when they were lifted up from the land, the wheels were lifted up beside them — for the ruach of the living creature was in the wheels.

paragraphs.commentary: **The verbatim restatement.** V21 repeats v20's claim — *ruach ha-chayyah ba-ofannim* — at the end of the verse, this time inside a larger description of synchronized motion (going, standing, being lifted up). The repetition is structural: the chapter is making absolutely sure the reader sees that the apparatus is a unified system.

paragraphs.text: וּדְמ֞וּת עַל־רָאשֵׁ֤י הַחַיָּה֙ רָקִ֔יעַ כְּעֵ֖ין הַקֶּ֣רַח הַנּוֹרָ֑א נָט֥וּי עַל־רָאשֵׁיהֶ֖ם מִלְמָֽעְלָה׃

i18n.en: Above the heads of the living creature was the likeness of a dome, like the look of awesome ice, spread above their heads from above.

paragraphs.commentary: **The raqia returns.** *Raqia* — the same word as in Genesis 1:6-8, where the WoH translation uses *dome* (the kiln-hammered solid vault separating the upper and lower waters). Ezekiel's raqia is positioned *above the heads* of the chayyot — not the cosmic vault of Genesis but a smaller portable platform, *ke-ein ha-qerach ha-nora* (*like the look of awesome ice / crystal*). The cognate Akkadian and Ugaritic words for *raqia* denote *something hammered thin* (Job 37:18 uses the verbal form for hammering bronze mirrors); *qerach* (קֶרַח) is *ice / crystal* — transparent, hard, surface-like. // The chapter is reusing Gen 1's cosmological vocabulary for a localized object. The throne-platform raqia (Ezek 1:22) and the cosmic raqia (Gen 1:6-8) share a noun; the chapter is positioning the chayyot-and-wheels system as carrying *a portable raqia* of the same kind as the cosmic vault. The Wheel of Heaven lens reads the structural parallel.

paragraphs.text: וְתַ֙חַת֙ הָרָקִ֔יעַ כַּנְפֵיהֶ֣ם יְשָׁר֔וֹת אִשָּׁ֖ה אֶל־אֲחוֹתָ֑הּ לְאִ֗ישׁ שְׁתַּ֤יִם מְכַסּוֹת֙ לָהֵ֔נָּה וּלְאִ֗ישׁ שְׁתַּ֤יִם מְכַסּוֹת֙ לָהֵ֔נָּה אֵ֖ת גְּוִיֹּתֵיהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: Under the dome their wings were straight, one to another; each had two wings covering them, and each had two wings covering their bodies.

paragraphs.text: וָאֶשְׁמַ֣ע אֶת־ק֣וֹל כַּנְפֵיהֶ֡ם כְּקוֹל֩ מַ֨יִם רַבִּ֤ים כְּקוֹל־שַׁדַּי֙ בְּלֶכְתָּ֔ן ק֥וֹל הֲמֻלָּ֖ה כְּק֣וֹל מַחֲנֶ֑ה בְּעָמְדָ֖ם תְּרַפֶּ֥ינָה כַנְפֵיהֶֽן׃

i18n.en: I heard the sound of their wings like the sound of many waters, like the voice of Shaddai when they went — a tumultuous sound like the sound of an army; when they stood, they would let down their wings.

paragraphs.commentary: **Four sound-similes for a single phenomenon.** The chapter stacks four comparisons for the sound the wings made when in motion: (1) *qol mayim rabbim* — *the sound of many waters* (roaring water, ocean-like); (2) *qol Shaddai* — *the voice of Shaddai* (the Hebrew Bible's most-powerful divine voice register; Shaddai is the patriarchal divine name, often translated 'the Almighty'); (3) *qol hamullah* — *a tumultuous sound* (chaotic loud noise); (4) *qol machaneh* — *the sound of an army* (military encampment, the roar of massed people). // *Qol Shaddai* is the central simile: the wings make a sound like the divine voice itself. The chapter is staging an auditory transition from the chayyot-as-described to the divine-presence-being-approached. The voice from above the raqia in v25 will land in this acoustic register.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִי־ק֕וֹל מֵעַ֕ל לָרָקִ֖יעַ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עַל־רֹאשָׁ֑ם בְּעָמְדָ֖ם תְּרַפֶּ֥ינָה כַנְפֵיהֶֽן׃

i18n.en: And a voice came from above the dome that was over their heads; when they stood, they would let down their wings.

paragraphs.commentary: **The voice from above the raqia.** A second sound is introduced — separate from the wing-sounds of v24. *Qol me'al la-raqia* — *a voice from above the dome*. The wings' sound was below the raqia (v23); this new sound originates *above* it. The chapter is staging a vertical acoustic-geometry: the chayyot's wings sound below, a voice sounds above. The 'voice from above' belongs to whatever sits above the raqia — the throne and figure of v26-28.

paragraphs.text: וּמִמַּ֗עַל לָרָקִ֙יעַ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עַל־רֹאשָׁ֔ם כְּמַרְאֵ֥ה אֶֽבֶן־סַפִּ֖יר דְּמ֣וּת כִּסֵּ֑א וְעַל֙ דְּמ֣וּת הַכִּסֵּ֔א דְּמ֞וּת כְּמַרְאֵ֥ה אָדָ֛ם עָלָ֖יו מִלְמָֽעְלָה׃

i18n.en: Above the dome over their heads, like the appearance of sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne; and on the likeness of the throne, the likeness of an appearance like human, on it from above.

paragraphs.commentary: **The throne, and the figure on it.** *K'mar'eh eben-sappir demut kisse* — *like the appearance of sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne*. *Sappir* (סַפִּיר) is the Hebrew Bible's word for *sapphire* or *lapis lazuli* — the blue gemstone associated with divine throne-platforms in ANE iconography. Ex 24:10 also uses *eben sappir* (the same compound) for what Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the seventy elders saw under YHWH's feet at Sinai: *and there was under his feet as it were a paved work of sapphire stone, and as it were the very heaven for clearness*. Ezekiel is reusing the Sinai-throne vocabulary. // *Demut k'mar'eh adam alav milmaalah* — *the likeness of an appearance like human, on it from above*. The chapter's hedging-formulae stack here: *demut k'mar'eh* — *likeness of an appearance* — followed by *adam* (human). What sits on the throne has the *appearance of the likeness of a human-figure* — three layers of qualifying language, the most cautious description the chapter offers. The figure is human-shaped, but the chapter does not assert that it IS human.

paragraphs.text: וָאֵ֣רֶא ׀ כְּעֵ֣ין חַשְׁמַ֗ל כְּמַרְאֵה־אֵ֤שׁ בֵּֽית־לָהּ֙ סָבִ֔יב מִמַּרְאֵ֥ה מָתְנָ֖יו וּלְמָ֑עְלָה וּמִמַּרְאֵ֤ה מָתְנָיו֙ וּלְמַ֔טָּה רָאִ֙יתִי֙ כְּמַרְאֵה־אֵ֔שׁ וְנֹ֥גַֽהּ ל֖וֹ סָבִֽיב׃

i18n.en: I saw — like the look of *chashmal*, like the appearance of fire encased around — from the appearance of his loins and upward; and from the appearance of his loins and downward I saw like the appearance of fire, and brightness around him.

paragraphs.commentary: **The figure described in two halves.** From the loins upward: *ke-ein chashmal* — *like the look of chashmal* (the same word as v4) — *k'mar'eh esh bet-lah saviv* — *like the appearance of fire encased around*. From the loins downward: *k'mar'eh esh* — *like the appearance of fire*. And *nogah lo saviv* — *brightness around him* — recapitulating the descriptor used of the storm-cloud apparatus in v4. // The figure is described in the same metallic-luminous-fiery vocabulary as the apparatus that carries him — *chashmal* matches v4, *esh* (fire) and *nogah* (brightness) match v4 and v13. The chapter is positioning the figure on the throne as the same kind of phenomenon as the chayyot-and-wheels below. The figure is *not* qualitatively different from the apparatus; both are described in the same technical vocabulary.

paragraphs.text: כְּמַרְאֵ֣ה הַקֶּ֡שֶׁת אֲשֶׁר֩ יִֽהְיֶ֨ה בֶעָנָ֜ן בְּי֣וֹם הַגֶּ֗שֶׁם כֵּ֣ן מַרְאֵ֤ה הַנֹּ֙גַהּ֙ סָבִ֔יב ה֕וּא מַרְאֵ֖ה דְּמ֣וּת כְּבוֹד־יְהוָ֑ה וָֽאֶרְאֶה֙ וָאֶפֹּ֣ל עַל־פָּנַ֔י וָאֶשְׁמַ֖ע ק֥וֹל מְדַבֵּֽר׃

i18n.en: Like the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud on a day of rain — so was the appearance of the brightness around. This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of YHWH. When I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard a voice speaking.

paragraphs.commentary: **The closing identification, and the closing posture.** Three things happen in this verse. // First, *k'mar'eh ha-qeshet asher yihyeh be-anan b'yom ha-geshem* — *like the appearance of the bow (qeshet) that is in the cloud on a day of rain*. The bow / rainbow simile is the chapter's final descriptor of the brightness around the figure. *Qeshet* is the same word as in Gen 9:13-16, the bow YHWH places in the cloud as the sign of the post-Flood covenant (see glossary entry `qashti-be-anan`). The chapter is doing structural reverberation: the rainbow that was the covenant-sign with Noah and all flesh is here the descriptor of the radiance around the figure on the throne. The chapter is signaling that what Ezekiel sees is *of the same kind* as what was promised after the Flood — the post-Flood YHWH himself, in the exilic vision. // Second, *hu mar'eh demut kvod YHWH* — *this was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of YHWH*. The chapter's most-extended hedging formula: *appearance of the likeness of the glory*. Three layers of qualifying language. Ezekiel does not identify what he saw as YHWH directly; he identifies it as the *appearance of the likeness of the glory* of YHWH. The *kavod* (כָּבוֹד) is the technical Hebrew Bible term for the radiant, visible *presence-manifestation* of YHWH — the cloud-and-fire of the Exodus (Ex 13:21-22, 24:16-17), the cloud-filled tabernacle (Ex 40:34-35), the cloud-filled Temple (1 Kgs 8:10-11). The chapter is identifying the chayyot-and-wheels-and-throne-and-figure complex as the *kavod-YHWH* — the technical presence-manifestation, not the divine essence directly. // Third, *va-eppol al panai va-eshma qol medabber* — *I fell on my face, and I heard a voice speaking*. The standard prophetic-encounter response (cf. Daniel 8:17, 10:9 for parallels). The chapter ends mid-encounter — chapter 2 will record what the voice says (the prophetic commissioning of Ezekiel). The vision is now established; the message follows.
